blocks.text: Nigeria's population is often quoted as "about 220 million". Nobody means exactly 220,000,000 people. Approximation is how we report numbers honestly — and standard form is how we write the very large and very small ones without drowning in zeros.

blocks.markdown:
There are two different ways WAEC asks you to approximate, and mixing them up costs easy marks.

**Decimal places (d.p.)** counts digits **after** the decimal point.

**Significant figures (s.f.)** counts digits starting from the first **non-zero** digit, wherever it happens to be.

blocks.title: Significant figure
blocks.text: A significant figure is any digit that carries information about the size of a number. Counting starts at the first non-zero digit from the left. Leading zeros are never significant, so in $0.004628$ the first significant figure is the 4.

items: Identify the last digit you are allowed to keep.
Look at the very next digit only — never at the digits beyond it.
If that next digit is 5 or more, add 1 to the digit you are keeping; otherwise leave it.
Fill any places between your rounded digit and the decimal point with zeros so the number keeps its size.

steps.text: The leading zeros are not significant. The first significant figure is 4, the second is 6, the third is 2.
The next digit after the third significant figure is 8.
Since 8 is 5 or more, round the 2 up to 3.
Keep all the leading zeros so the number does not change in size.

blocks.markdown:
### Standard form

Every number can be written as

$$A \times 10^{n}$$

where $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ is a whole number. The condition on $A$ is strict: $45.3 \times 10^{-6}$ is **not** in standard form because 45.3 is bigger than 10.

A **positive** power of ten means a large number; a **negative** power means a small one. The power counts how many places the decimal point has to move.

blocks.caption: The sign of the power tells you which way the point moved

blocks.title: Multiplying in standard form
blocks.prompt: Evaluate (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²), leaving your answer in standard form.

steps.text: Multiply the number parts and the powers of ten separately.
Add the indices when multiplying powers of the same base.
12 is not between 1 and 10, so rewrite it as 1.2 × 10¹.
Add the indices again to finish.

blocks.caption: Percentage error always divides by the true (exact) value

blocks.title: Do not round twice
blocks.text: Round only once, at the very end, and only using the digit immediately after your cut-off. Rounding 24.3856 to 2 d.p. by first going to 24.4 and then writing 24.40 gives the wrong answer; the correct value is 24.39.

points: Decimal places count digits after the point; significant figures count from the first non-zero digit.
Round using only the single digit immediately after your cut-off point.
Positive powers of ten mean large numbers, negative powers mean small numbers.
When multiplying or dividing in standard form, handle the number parts and the powers separately.
Percentage error divides the size of the error by the true value, then multiplies by 100%.
